Note: Use Genau to agree precisely with what someone has just said.
ExampleGerman: Der Zug fährt um acht. – Genau.
ExampleEnglish: The train leaves at eight. – Exactly.

Note: A short way to confirm that information is correct.
ExampleGerman: Der Laden ist heute geschlossen. – Stimmt, heute ist Sonntag.
ExampleEnglish: The shop is closed today. – That’s right, today is Sunday.

Note: Use it to agree readily. In other contexts, klar means clear.
ExampleGerman: Kannst du mir kurz helfen? – Klar.
ExampleEnglish: Can you help me for a moment? – Sure.

Note: A friendly affirmative; tone can make it sound impatient, so keep the intonation warm.
ExampleGerman: Darf ich das Fenster öffnen? – Natürlich.
ExampleEnglish: May I open the window? – Of course.

Note: Signals possibility, not a definite yes.
ExampleGerman: Vielleicht besuchen wir am Samstag den Markt.
ExampleEnglish: Maybe we’ll visit the market on Saturday.

Note: Often placed at the start of a sentence to soften disappointing news.
ExampleGerman: Leider kann ich heute nicht länger bleiben.
ExampleEnglish: Unfortunately, I can’t stay longer today.

Note: Expresses mild disappointment or sympathy.
ExampleGerman: Du kannst nicht mitkommen? – Schade!
ExampleEnglish: You can’t come with us? – That’s a shame!

Note: A natural, concise response to an invitation or request. Also common in the phrase gern haben.
ExampleGerman: Möchtest du einen Tee? – Ja, gern.
ExampleEnglish: Would you like some tea? – Yes, please.

Note: The person is in the dative: Der Termin passt mir. The phrase can also mean that something fits physically.
ExampleGerman: Passt dir der Termin morgen? – Ja, das passt mir gut.
ExampleEnglish: Does the appointment tomorrow work for you? – Yes, that works well for me.

Note: Confirms that you understand or accept a plan.
ExampleGerman: Wir treffen uns um sechs vor dem Kino. – Alles klar.
ExampleEnglish: We’ll meet outside the cinema at six. – Got it.

Note: A common response to thanks, apologies, or small requests.
ExampleGerman: Entschuldigung für die Verspätung. – Kein Problem.
ExampleEnglish: Sorry I’m late. – No problem.

Note: Accepts a suggestion, sometimes after a little hesitation.
ExampleGerman: Na gut, dann nehmen wir den nächsten Bus.
ExampleEnglish: All right then, we’ll take the next bus.

Note: Use with rising intonation when you did not hear or understand. It is more polite than Was? in formal situations.
ExampleGerman: Wie bitte? Könnten Sie das bitte wiederholen?
ExampleEnglish: Pardon? Could you please repeat that?

Note: Common in conversation. For a more neutral tone, say: Ich weiß es nicht.
ExampleGerman: Weißt du, wann der Zug kommt? – Keine Ahnung.
ExampleEnglish: Do you know when the train arrives? – I have no idea.

Note: A friendly farewell to one person you address with du.
ExampleGerman: Danke für den schönen Abend. Mach’s gut!
ExampleEnglish: Thanks for a lovely evening. Take care!

Note: A useful full sentence when you need someone to repeat information. Use Sie for formal address.
ExampleGerman: Entschuldigung, könnten Sie die Adresse bitte wiederholen?
ExampleEnglish: Excuse me, could you please repeat the address?

EnglishMeanings: Yes, actually (reply to a negative question)
Note: Doch can contradict a negative statement. Its meaning depends strongly on the sentence; it is not a general translation for however.
ExampleGerman: Du hast heute keine Zeit? – Doch, ab drei Uhr.
ExampleEnglish: You don’t have time today? – I do, from three o’clock.

Note: The usual spelling is two words: na ja. It often introduces a hesitant or qualified answer.
ExampleGerman: Na ja, der Film war ganz gut, aber etwas lang.
ExampleEnglish: Well, the film was quite good, but a little long.

Note: A short reaction to surprising news. As an adjective, echt can also mean genuine or real.
ExampleGerman: Ich habe den Job bekommen. – Echt? Glückwunsch!
ExampleEnglish: I got the job. – Really? Congratulations!

Note: Eben has several meanings. In this response it signals agreement; in other sentences it can mean just or a moment ago.
ExampleGerman: Man sollte vorher reservieren. – Eben.
ExampleEnglish: You should reserve in advance. – Exactly.

Note: Often introduces a question or thought that differs slightly from the current topic.
ExampleGerman: Was machst du eigentlich am Wochenende?
ExampleEnglish: What are you doing this weekend, by the way?

Note: At the start of a spoken sentence, also often introduces a conclusion or next step. It does not usually mean also in English.
ExampleGerman: Also, fangen wir mit der ersten Aufgabe an.
ExampleEnglish: So, let’s start with the first task.

Note: Use it to add a side note or introduce a related new topic.
ExampleGerman: Übrigens, deine Schwester hat gestern angerufen.
ExampleEnglish: By the way, your sister called yesterday.

Note: With a question intonation, it shows surprise. In a statement, wirklich means really or truly.
ExampleGerman: Sie zieht nach Berlin. – Wirklich?
ExampleEnglish: She’s moving to Berlin. – Really?

Note: Shows that something is true regardless of another circumstance.
ExampleGerman: Ich nehme sowieso den Bus.
ExampleEnglish: I’m taking the bus anyway.

Note: Highlights a positive or important fact despite a drawback.
ExampleGerman: Der Weg war weit, aber immerhin war das Wetter schön.
ExampleEnglish: The journey was long, but at least the weather was nice.

Note: As a modal particle, halt presents something as a fact or an accepted limitation. Its meaning is not the same as the verb halten.
ExampleGerman: Der Laden ist geschlossen. Dann gehen wir halt morgen.
ExampleEnglish: The shop is closed. Then we’ll just go tomorrow.

Note: In requests, mal often makes the sentence sound more relaxed. It does not have one fixed translation here.
ExampleGerman: Kannst du mir mal kurz helfen?
ExampleEnglish: Could you give me a hand for a moment?

EnglishMeanings: (softens or adds interest to a question)
Note: In questions, denn is a modal particle and is usually not translated as because.
ExampleGerman: Was machst du denn heute Abend?
ExampleEnglish: So, what are you doing this evening?

Note: A common reassuring phrase. Here schon does not mean already.
ExampleGerman: Mach dir keine Sorgen. Das wird schon.
ExampleEnglish: Don’t worry. It’ll be all right.

Note: Gar strengthens a negative. Learn it in the phrase gar nicht rather than on its own.
ExampleGerman: Der Weg ist gar nicht weit.
ExampleEnglish: The way isn’t far at all.

Note: Although introduces a contrast. In a subordinate clause, the conjugated verb goes to the end.
ExampleGerman: Obwohl es regnet, gehen wir spazieren.
ExampleEnglish: Although it’s raining, we’re going for a walk.

Note: Deshalb introduces a result. If it comes first, the conjugated verb follows it: Deshalb bleibe ich …
ExampleGerman: Ich bin müde. Deshalb gehe ich früh ins Bett.
ExampleEnglish: I’m tired. That’s why I’m going to bed early.

Note: Use it to replace an expected or suggested action.
ExampleGerman: Wir fahren nicht mit dem Auto. Stattdessen nehmen wir den Zug.
ExampleEnglish: We aren’t going by car. Instead, we’re taking the train.

Note: Introduces an action that happens despite what was just mentioned. The conjugated verb follows trotzdem when it starts the sentence.
ExampleGerman: Es ist kalt. Trotzdem gehen die Kinder nach draußen.
ExampleEnglish: It’s cold. Even so, the children are going outside.

Note: Often adds a qualification or contrast. The exact force depends on context and intonation.
ExampleGerman: Das Hotel ist schön, allerdings ist es ziemlich teuer.
ExampleEnglish: The hotel is lovely, though it is quite expensive.

Note: Sets a minimum or limits what you are claiming.
ExampleGerman: Zumindest haben wir es versucht.
ExampleEnglish: At least we tried.

EnglishMeanings: On the one hand … on the other hand …
Note: Use the paired expressions to compare two sides of an issue.
ExampleGerman: Einerseits möchte ich reisen, andererseits muss ich sparen.
ExampleEnglish: On the one hand I’d like to travel; on the other hand I need to save money.

Note: Ob introduces an indirect yes-or-no question; the conjugated verb goes to the end.
ExampleGerman: Ich weiß nicht, ob der Supermarkt noch geöffnet ist.
ExampleEnglish: I don’t know whether the supermarket is still open.

Note: Use this pair to acknowledge one point and then contrast it with another.
ExampleGerman: Der Weg ist zwar weit, aber die Aussicht lohnt sich.
ExampleEnglish: The way is a long one, but the view is worth it.

Note: Returns to the main point or states what is certain after considering other details.
ExampleGerman: Ob es regnet, weiß ich nicht. Jedenfalls nehme ich einen Schirm mit.
ExampleEnglish: I don’t know whether it will rain. In any case, I’m taking an umbrella.

EnglishMeanings: To feel like doing or having something
Note: Use auf with the accusative noun: Lust auf einen Kaffee. Before an infinitive, use Lust haben, etwas zu tun.
ExampleGerman: Hast du Lust auf einen Spaziergang?
ExampleEnglish: Do you feel like going for a walk?

Note: Casual spoken German. Avoid it in formal emails, work situations, or with people you address as Sie.
ExampleGerman: Hast du Bock auf Pizza?
ExampleEnglish: Are you up for pizza?

Note: A strong yes or a way to emphasize that something will happen.
ExampleGerman: Kommst du morgen mit? – Auf jeden Fall!
ExampleEnglish: Are you coming with us tomorrow? – Definitely!

Note: A firm negative. It is the opposite of auf jeden Fall.
ExampleGerman: Soll ich ohne Ticket fahren? – Auf keinen Fall!
ExampleEnglish: Should I travel without a ticket? – Absolutely not!

Note: Use it to warn someone or to get their attention before explaining something.
ExampleGerman: Pass auf! Die Stufe ist sehr hoch.
ExampleEnglish: Watch out! The step is very high.

Note: A clear, friendly way to suggest doing something together.
ExampleGerman: Lass uns nach der Arbeit einen Kaffee trinken.
ExampleEnglish: Let’s have a coffee after work.

Note: Reassures someone that a small mistake or inconvenience is okay.
ExampleGerman: Ich habe den Namen vergessen. – Macht nichts.
ExampleEnglish: I forgot the name. – That’s all right.

Note: Often used to accept an apology or signal that no further explanation is needed.
ExampleGerman: Tut mir leid, dass ich dich warten ließ. – Schon gut.
ExampleEnglish: Sorry I kept you waiting. – No worries.

Note: A friendly response to Danke. Danke schön and Gern geschehen are also common.
ExampleGerman: Vielen Dank für Ihre Hilfe. – Nichts zu danken.
ExampleEnglish: Thank you very much for your help. – You’re welcome.

Note: An energetic prompt to start or hurry. Tone determines whether it sounds encouraging or impatient.
ExampleGerman: Der Film fängt gleich an. Los, wir müssen gehen!
ExampleEnglish: The film is about to start. Come on, we have to go!

Note: Very informal reaction to something surprising or intense. Avoid it in formal situations.
ExampleGerman: Du bist zu Fuß bis hierher gelaufen? Krass!
ExampleEnglish: You walked all the way here? Wow!

Note: A playful blend of ja and nein. It signals a qualified or mixed answer, not a clear yes.
ExampleGerman: Hat dir der Film gefallen? – Jein. Das Ende war gut, der Rest nicht.
ExampleEnglish: Did you like the film? – Yes and no. The ending was good; the rest wasn’t.

Note: A greeting or farewell used especially in Bavaria, Austria, and parts of southern Germany.
ExampleGerman: Servus, Anna! Wie geht’s?
ExampleEnglish: Hi, Anna! How are you?

Note: A greeting common in northern Germany. It can be used throughout the day, not only in the morning.
ExampleGerman: Moin! Ist hier noch ein Platz frei?
ExampleEnglish: Hi! Is this seat free?

Note: A casual greeting among friends. Use Wie geht es Ihnen? in formal situations.
ExampleGerman: Hey, was geht? Hast du heute Abend Zeit?
ExampleEnglish: Hey, what’s up? Are you free this evening?

Note: A shortened form of Schön wäre es. It responds to a wish or suggestion that seems unlikely.
ExampleGerman: Morgen ist bestimmt frei. – Schön wär’s!
ExampleEnglish: Tomorrow will surely be a day off. – I wish!
